description: Builds the §10.7 push path: relays store signed push registrations and send a wake signal through APNs, FCM and WebPush when a message arrives for a registered routing ID, and devices accept the wake, connect, and pull pending envelopes. The keri workstream owns the one function that checks a registration's signature against the identity's key state (§10.7.1 step 3); this PRD owns that function's interface, the relay code that calls it, and the error mapping (PUSH-005). Until keri replaces the stub body, every relay with push enabled answers 5003 and accepts no registration. PUSH-001 to PUSH-003 amend the specs and ADRs first, so each code story cites a section that already states its requirement. Alec ruled on 2026-10-12 that a registration lists routing IDs in place of plaintext context IDs (D5), that the registration key includes the device token so that each device registers separately (D6), and that WebPush is specified fully in a later gate (D3), which gate-push-webpush holds (PUSH-021 to PUSH-024). Alec ruled on 2026-10-24 that the protocol drops the per-device-token push rate limit ("I feel like we should remove the limit", then "So remove it and b done yes?"), so this PRD dropped PUSH-009, the story titled "Rate limit of one push per 30 s per token". The reasoning Alec accepted: push credentials belong to each app developer, so a flood of wakes uses up only that developer's own provider quota, and any limit is that developer's relay policy, which §10.7.1 step 5 **Relay limits** permits and the protocol does not set.

stories.title: Amend the push payload and the device receipt rule per platform
stories.description:
Step 5 of §10.7.1, the push registration protocol, fixed the relay's push payload as one byte string, `{ "scp": 1 }`, while ADR-025, the Apple platform adapter, fixed the APNs payload as `{"aps": {"content-available": 1}}`. Both texts claimed to define the exact bytes the relay sends to APNs, and iOS wakes a background app only for a payload that carries `aps.content-available`, so the §10.7.1 text was wrong for APNs. ADR-027, the Android platform adapter, gave the FCM sender a body that addressed the device through the legacy FCM API's top-level `to` field, which the FCM HTTP v1 API rejects. ADR-025 acceptance criterion 4 also made `handleNotification` compare raw bytes, which no code on the iOS delivery path can run, because iOS hands the app a parsed `userInfo` dictionary.

This story replaces §10.7.1 step 5 with a wake-signal table holding one request per platform (APNs and FCM; PUSH-021 adds the WebPush row) and adds a device receipt rule per platform. The plan's decisions D1, D2 and D10 govern: D1b, the device accepts an APNs wake only when the parsed dictionary has exactly the key `aps`, and `aps` has exactly `content-available` = 1; D2b, every FCM wake carries `android.priority: HIGH`; D10, the app calls the Rust core and the Rust core calls the UniFFI `PushProvider` callback. ADR-006, the in-memory platform adapter, and ADR-025 cite the §10.7.1 table rather than restating the bytes. The SCP-096 action item that asked for an encrypted context identifier in the APNs payload contradicted §10.7, which forbids any context in a push payload, so this story removes it. Doc comments in `scp-protocol`, `scp-platform` and the Kotlin Android adapter that restated `{ "scp": 1 }` or the legacy FCM body now cite the table. Swift and Kotlin code changes belong to PUSH-017 and PUSH-018.
acceptanceCriteria: §10.7.1 step 5 contains one table with the rows APNs and FCM, each giving the request body and the headers.
The string `{ "scp": 1 }` no longer appears in §10.7.1.
`git grep -n '"scp": 1' -- .docs/specs` returns nothing; §16.12.5 cites the §10.7.1 step 5 table instead of restating payload bytes.
ADR-025 acceptance criterion 4 checks a parsed dictionary and contains no "whitespace outside string literals" clause.
ADR-027 contains no `"to":` key.
ADR-006 and ADR-025 cite §10.7.1 rather than restating the bytes.
The SCP-096 action item in `.docs/prds/main.json` no longer mentions context_id.

ADR-025 and ADR-027 state the D10 call order: `push_enable(provider)` calls `registerPush()` and publishes a signed registration; `push_handle_wake(payload)` calls `handleNotification(payload)`, then runs relay catch-up under a deadline and returns `WakeOutcome`.
§10.7.1 step 5 states the APNs receipt rule (exactly the key `aps`, and `aps` exactly `content-available` = 1) and the FCM receipt rule (`scp` equals the string `"1"`).
The FCM row of the §10.7.1 table sets `android.priority` to `HIGH` and carries no `notification` key.
`python3.12 scripts/check-doc-citations.py` passes.
actionItems: Replace §10.7.1 step 5's payload sentence with the wake-signal table and the device receipt rule.
Amend ADR-025: the Decision's push paragraph, criterion 4 (parsed-dictionary rule, relay item, call order) and criterion 7's test item.
Amend ADR-027: the Decision's FCM items, the `AndroidPushProvider.kt` code block (FCM HTTP v1 body) and criterion 10 (call order).
Amend ADR-006's `InMemoryPush` bullet to cite the §10.7.1 table.
Rewrite the SCP-096 action item so that it names no context identifier.
Point the stale doc comments in `push.rs`, `push_provider.rs`, `AndroidPushProvider.kt` and its test at the §10.7.1 table.

stories.title: Amend the push encoding, freshness, relay exception and privacy statement
stories.description: Fixes the stale copies and gaps the plan's decisions D4, D6a, D7, D8 and D9 found in the push wire format. §22.11.4, the push wire table, encodes `contexts` as length-prefixed strings with no element count, while §9.5.1, which §22.11.4 cites, requires a 4-byte big-endian element count before every repeated field; §9.5.1 governs. §10.7.1 restates the registration struct with types that drifted from the §22.11.4 wire table, so §10.7.1 cites §22.11.4 instead. §9.5.2 gets one signed-structure table per push separator (`SCP-PUSH-REGISTER-V1:` and `SCP-PUSH-DEREGISTER-V1:`); both preimages end with the canonical `relay_url` under §9.5.1's length-prefixed rule, so a signature binds to one relay (D8); the V1 encoding is fixed in place without a V2 bump, because no code has ever signed with V1 (D4b). §9.18.2 registers the reserved routing derivation `SHA-256("scp-push-registration" || relay_url)` and the canonical form of `relay_url`. §9.5.2 lists both push messages among the preimages that take an identity identifier: the `registrant` field is encoded as the 56-byte `scp:` text form of the SCP-308 S1 `Identifier` under §9.5.1's length-prefixed rule, and the separators stay V1 when S1 changes the bytes inside the length prefix. ADR-004, the native relay protocol, lists push interception as a second narrow exception to relay opacity, registers the push wire codes, the timestamp skew window, and the rule that the relay never stores or delivers a push message as a blob. The §10.7.1 storage paragraph states that a relay holding a push registration learns the identity, its platform token and the routing IDs listed for it (D7), and §9.10.4 lists that linkage as a residual. §17.17, capability selection, and the ADR-062 classification table add rows for the push registration store (shipped arm SQLite only; the in-memory arm compiles only under `testing`), the push senders, and the push signature verifier.
acceptanceCriteria: §22.11.4 states the BE32 element count for the repeated field.
§9.5.2 has one table per push separator.
§9.5.2's list of preimages that take an identifier names `PushRegistration` and `PushDeregistration`, with `registrant` encoded as the 56-byte `scp:` text form under the length-prefixed rule.
§9.5.2 states that the push separators stay V1 when SCP-308 S1 changes the bytes inside the `registrant` length prefix.

Both §9.5.2 push preimages end with the canonical `relay_url` as a 4-byte big-endian length and its UTF-8 bytes, and §22.11.4 and §10.7.1 state that the relay verifies against its own canonical URL, so a message signed for a different relay URL fails verification and gets 4060.

§9.18.2 registers the reserved routing derivation and the canonical form of `relay_url` (indicator: the WebSocket URL the client dialed, scheme and host lowercased, default port elided, no trailing slash).
§10.7.1 cites §22.11.4 rather than restating the struct.
ADR-004 lists two narrow exceptions, the codes 4060-4064 and 5003-5004, the skew window, and the rule that push messages are never stored or delivered as blobs.
ADR-004 states that a relay whose push role is `Disabled` rejects any PUBLISH to the reserved routing ID with code 4063.
The §10.7.1 storage paragraph states the D7 linkage, and §9.10.4 lists it as a residual.

§17.17 and the ADR-062 table each have rows for the push store, the push senders and the push verifier, each with its classification; the push store row states that the shipped arm is SQLite and the in-memory arm compiles only under `testing`.
`python3.12 scripts/check-doc-citations.py` passes.
actionItems: Add the element count to §22.11.4 and replace §10.7.1's struct with a citation of §22.11.4.
Add the two §9.5.2 tables and the §9.18.2 registration.
Amend ADR-004 with the second exception, the wire codes, the skew window and the no-blob rule.
Amend the §10.7.1 storage paragraph and the §9.10.4 residuals.
Add the push rows to §17.17 and to the ADR-062 classification table.

stories.title: Routing IDs, a per-device registration key, and the registrant field
stories.description: Applies Alec's 2026-10-12 rulings on D5 and D6, and keri's ruling on the identity field. D5: §10.7.1 carries plaintext `contexts: Vec<ContextId>`, which hands the relay the context ID that §9.10.4 forbids it to learn; the registration carries `routing_ids: Vec<[u8; 32]>` instead, and an empty list is invalid. D6: §10.7.1 keys a registration by identity and platform, so a second device on the same platform replaces the first, while §10.8.1 gives each device its own MLS leaf; a registration is keyed by (identity identifier, platform, token), `PushDeregistration` carries `token`, and the relay caps the registrations per identity identifier. Identity field: both messages name the signer `registrant`, typed `Identifier` as SCP-308 S1 defines it, and every text this story writes calls it the identity identifier. Alec ruled on D3 (WebPush) to specify it fully in a later gate; PUSH-021 writes that spec text, so this story leaves the WebPush enum entry and tag `0x03` as they are.
acceptanceCriteria: §22.11.4 lists `routing_ids` with a fixed 32-byte element type, and states that an empty list is invalid.
The §22.11.4 tables of both messages name the signer field `registrant: Identifier`, citing SCP-308 S1, and `registrant` is the only identity field in either table.
`PushDeregistration` contains `token` in its table and its preimage.
§10.7.1 states the (identity identifier, platform, token) registration key and the per-identity cap (indicator: 16).
§10.7.1 no longer contains `contexts: Vec<ContextId>`.
`python3.12 scripts/check-doc-citations.py` passes.
actionItems: Replace `contexts` with `routing_ids` in §22.11.4 and §10.7.1.
Rename the signer field to `registrant: Identifier` and add `token` to `PushDeregistration`.
State the registration key and the per-identity cap in §10.7.1.

stories.title: Push wire types, canonical signing bytes and test vectors
stories.description: Fixes the `PushRegistration` and `PushDeregistration` field types to match the §22.11.4 wire table, and adds the one canonical-bytes function per message, which takes the canonical relay URL the preimage ends with (§9.5.2), the MessagePack encoding, and the reserved routing ID derivation. The keri workstream's verifier computes each preimage through these canonical-bytes functions, so no other code builds a push preimage. Both messages carry the signer in `registrant`. Until SCP-308 S1 lands the `Identifier` type, `registrant` holds today's did:dht string; the code lags the spec here, and the field's doc comment and this story's PR body record that gap. When S1 lands, the bytes inside the `registrant` length prefix change and the separators stay V1. The `crates/scp-core/src/lib.rs` re-export already exists; this story checks it. Protocol types only, so every integration-checklist row is n/a.
acceptanceCriteria: `push_registration_signing_bytes` and `push_deregistration_signing_bytes` each take the relay URL as a parameter, end the preimage with its canonical form under §9.5.1's length-prefixed rule, and produce bytes equal to golden vectors checked into `test_vectors.rs`.

A golden-vector case builds the preimage of one message for two relay URLs and shows that the two preimages differ; a second case shows that `WSS://Relay.Example:443/` and `wss://relay.example` yield one preimage.
These two functions are the only code that builds a push preimage: the PUSH-005 verifier interface and the PUSH-014 registrar both call them.
A test proves that two registrations whose routing-ID lists differ only in how elements split across the list produce different preimages.
`push_registration_routing_id("WSS://Relay.Example:443/")` equals the derivation for `wss://relay.example`.
Decoding a registration with zero routing IDs returns a typed error.
`PushRegistration` carries `routing_ids: Vec<[u8; 32]>` and `registrant`, `PushDeregistration` carries `registrant` and `token`, and `registrant` is the only identity field in either struct.
The `registrant` doc comment states that the field holds today's did:dht string until SCP-308 S1, and that S1 changes the bytes inside its length prefix without a separator bump.
The `Ed25519Signature` alias is gone.
actionItems: Retype the push message fields per §22.11.4.
Add the canonical-bytes functions, the MessagePack encoding and the reserved routing ID derivation.
Check in golden vectors.

stories.title: Push signature verifier trait and refusing stub (shared with keri)
stories.description:
Lands the push verifier interface that the keri workstream implements. keri's five constraints bind: (1) the verifier is an async trait object the relay receives by injection (`Arc<dyn PushSignatureVerifier>`, ADR-062); (2) `verify` takes the typed `PushRegistration` or `PushDeregistration`, never raw signed bytes, and computes the preimage through the PUSH-004 canonical-bytes function; (3) `verify` returns `Ok` carrying the verified identifier, typed `Identifier` (SCP-308 S1; today's did:dht string until S1 lands), or one of five rejections: identifier unresolvable, key state unavailable (retryable), signature invalid, key not `Current` in `#active`, and malformed; (4) no allow-all verifier exists, even behind `testing`; (5) keri builds its verifier body after its identifier story and the §9.7.4.2 R2, R3 and R8 key-state resolution land.

Before keri lands, the production struct `KelPushVerifier` refuses every message with a sixth error, verifier unavailable, which keri's body never returns; startup wires this struct whenever push is enabled, so every relay answers 5003 and accepts nothing unverified. keri has no story ID yet, so the stub carries `// Stub — see PUSH-005`, the form `.docs/standards/sdk-common.md` §Stub and Placeholder Policy requires; when keri files the story that replaces the stub body, the comment names that story instead. Tests use a verifier that checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies. The relay maps each rejection to one wire code of ADR-004's push table (PUSH-002): identifier unresolvable, signature invalid, key not Current in #active, and malformed map to 4060; key state unavailable, and a verifier call that exceeds its timeout (indicator: 10 s), map to 5004; verifier unavailable maps to 5003. Location `crates/scp-identity/src/push_verify.rs` is an indicator. keri reviews this PR and agrees to the signature before it merges.
acceptanceCriteria: `PushSignatureVerifier::verify` takes a typed `PushRegistration` or `PushDeregistration` and no byte-slice preimage parameter.

`verify` returns `Ok` carrying the verified identifier, or a `PushVerifyError` with exactly these rejections: identifier unresolvable, key state unavailable, signature invalid, key not `Current` in `#active`, malformed, and the stub-only verifier unavailable.
`KelPushVerifier::verify` returns `Err(VerifierUnavailable)` for every input, and the stub carries a `// Stub — see PUSH-005` comment.
The tests use a verifier that checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies, and that verifier lives behind `testing`.
That test verifier returns `SignatureInvalid` for a message signed by a key other than the one the test supplied.
No verifier that returns `Ok` without checking a signature exists in any build, `testing` included.
A function maps each `PushVerifyError` to its wire code (4060, 5003 or 5004), and a test covers every variant.
`scripts/check-shipped-feature-graph.sh` passes unchanged.
actionItems: Write the trait, the error enum and the stub struct.
Write the signature-checking test verifier under `testing`.
Write the error-to-wire-code mapping.
Get keri's agreement on the signature before merge.

stories.title: Relay interception of push registration and deregistration
stories.description: Adds `RelayConfig.push: PushRole` with the variants `Disabled` and `Enabled(PushServiceConfig)`. `Disabled` is the default, because it fails safe in the same way as `BridgeRole::Disabled` (ADR-052, the unified construction pattern, M2 and M4). `PushServiceConfig` holds the store, the `Arc<dyn PushSignatureVerifier>` and the configured senders; all three are required, with no defaults. `RelayConfig.relay_url` is a required `LiveRelayUrl` handle holding the relay URLs whose push routing IDs the relay reserves: the relay's §9.18.2 canonical URL, or, for a node, one entry per `SCPRelay` entry it publishes, each tier 3 entry with its `bridgeTarget` (PUSH-032). The relay derives each reserved push routing ID from its entry and rebuilds a preimage with the entry whose ID the PUBLISH arrived at (§10.7.1 steps 2 and 3). `RelayConfig` has no `Default` (M4 fires on `relay_url`), so no relay is built without a URL. A full node seeds the handle from its domain or its NAT tier address, and the NAT-tier task sets it before republishing on a tier change; the handle keeps a bounded list of retired routing IDs, and a PUBLISH to one is refused and never stored. The push gate runs in the PUBLISH handler of every relay transport that stores blobs (WebSocket, QUIC, UDP/DTLS and WebTransport) beside `did_slots.gate_publish`, after the rate-limit, size and TTL checks and before `storage.store`; the QUIC and WebTransport configurations carry clones of the same `relay_url` handle and the same `push` field, so every listener reads one handle and a change moves all of them at once. On any verifier rejection the relay stores nothing and changes nothing. File location `push_gate.rs` is an indicator. The operation is relay-internal and has no client dispatch, so the `pw` row is n/a.
acceptanceCriteria: A PUBLISH to the reserved routing ID never reaches `storage.store` or `deliver_to_subscribers`, whatever the result; tests prove this by querying and subscribing to the reserved routing ID afterwards.
A relay with `Disabled` returns 4063.
A relay wired with the stub `KelPushVerifier` returns 5003 for a valid registration and stores nothing.

A relay wired with the signature-checking test verifier of PUSH-005, which checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies and compiles only under `testing` stores a registration signed by the supplied key and returns success.
A relay wired with that test verifier returns 4060 for a registration signed by another key and stores nothing.
A relay returns 4062 for a timestamp outside the skew window (indicator: ±300 s) or not newer than the stored one.
A relay returns 4061 for a platform with no configured sender.
A valid deregistration removes exactly its own key.
The new codes are constants in `crates/scp-relay-client/src/error.rs`.

Every listener (WebSocket, QUIC, UDP/DTLS, WebTransport) reads the shared relay URL handle: after a URL change it intercepts the new reserved routing ID and refuses the previous one, storing nothing at either; a full node's NAT tier change to a URL with a §9.18.2 canonical form moves the handle, and a change to a tier 3 entry (one carrying `bridgeTarget`) moves it to that entry's tier 3 push routing ID (PUSH-032).

stories.title: Push sender seam, dispatcher, and deregistration after invalid-token failures
stories.description: The `PushSender` enum has the arms `Apns`, `Fcm` and, under `testing` only, `Recording`; a recording sender reports deliveries that never happened, so it is a nullifier and must stay out of the shipped feature graph. Each send returns `Delivered`, `InvalidToken`, `Transient` or `ConfigError`. A running push service comes only from `PushService::start(PushServiceConfig)` (ADR-052): the config is flat and holds no runtime state, and starting the service spawns its lookup and one drain per platform, so no relay can hold a dispatcher whose drain is not running, whichever transports it serves. Every transport's PUBLISH handler takes one path for every stored blob, DID record or opaque: deliver to subscribers, answer the publisher (the WebTransport handler returns its answer to the stream driver), then hand the routing ID to the service without waiting. The service looks up (platform, token) pairs for the routing ID off the async worker, in one query, and queues one job per token not already queued, up to a per-routing-ID bound (indicator: 1,000 live jobs) on a bounded per-platform queue (indicator: 10,000), so a slow push service stalls only its own platform and one routing ID's registrations cannot fill a queue. Both bounds and the drop of a wake beyond them are the ones §10.7.1 step 5 **Best-effort delivery** allows a relay. Each push client sets HTTP/2 keep-alive so a dead connection fails fast, and a `Transient` outcome backs off that platform's next send, except on WebPush, whose drain sends concurrently and whose sender backs off per endpoint origin (PUSH-022). A drop is logged at a bounded rate, with the running drop count. Only `InvalidToken` counts toward the 3 consecutive failures of §10.7.1; `Delivered` resets the counter, and a reset that fails to persist is carried so the next `InvalidToken` still counts from zero. The drain carries that reset in memory only, so a started service clears every stored invalid-token count before it queues its first job, and retries the clear until it lands; a restart therefore never lets a stale count remove a registration, and costs a token at most the 2 failures counted before it. At 3 the relay removes the registration. Tests register through the signature-checking test verifier of PUSH-005, which checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies and compiles only under `testing`. File location `push_dispatch.rs` is an indicator.
acceptanceCriteria: A publish to a registered routing ID enqueues exactly one job per matching token not already queued, up to the per-routing-ID bound that §10.7.1 step 5 **Best-effort delivery** allows; a flood of registrations on one routing ID leaves room for another routing ID's wake.
A full queue drops the job, as §10.7.1 step 5 **Best-effort delivery** allows, counts it in a log line written at a bounded rate, and the publish still succeeds.
Three `InvalidToken` outcomes in a row remove the registration.
`InvalidToken`, `InvalidToken`, `Delivered`, `InvalidToken` leaves the registration in place.
`Transient` and `ConfigError` never change the counter.
No push job carries the routing ID, the blob or the `registrant` identifier; a test inspects the job struct's fields.
Every test registration goes through the signature-checking test verifier of PUSH-005, which checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies and compiles only under `testing`.
The `Recording` arm compiles only under `testing`, and `scripts/check-shipped-feature-graph.sh` passes.

Every transport that stores blobs (WebSocket, QUIC, UDP, WebTransport) wakes on a DID-record publish and on an opaque publish, after subscriber delivery and after the reply wherever the handler writes the reply itself (the WebTransport handler returns its reply to the stream driver, so its wake is queued just before that return, without waiting); each test fails when that transport's notify is removed.
A push service that never answers on one platform delays no wake on the other platform, and no publish.
A `Delivered` whose counter reset fails to persist still breaks the run of failures.

Two `InvalidToken` outcomes, a `Delivered` whose counter reset fails to persist, a restart of the push service on the same store, then one `InvalidToken` leave the registration in place with a count of one; a service whose clear of the stored counts fails sends no wake until a retry of the clear lands.
actionItems: Write the sender enum, the push service with its per-platform queues and drains, and its start.
Run the notify after delivery and the reply in every transport's publish handler.
Write the invalid-token counter rules.

stories.title: APNs sender
stories.description: Sends the APNs row of the §10.7.1 step 5 wake-signal table over HTTP/2 to `api.push.apple.com`, or to `api.sandbox.push.apple.com` when the configured environment is `sandbox`. Authenticates with an ES256 provider JWT signed by the .p8 key through the `p256` crate the workspace already uses, carrying the key ID and team ID, refreshed every 50 minutes (indicator). Response mapping: 200 to `Delivered`; 410, or 400 with reason `BadDeviceToken`, to `InvalidToken`; 403 `InvalidProviderToken` or `ExpiredProviderToken` refreshes the JWT once, then `ConfigError`; 429 or 5xx to `Transient`; `DeviceTokenNotForTopic` to `InvalidToken`; `TopicDisallowed` to `ConfigError`. End-to-end tests register through the signature-checking test verifier of PUSH-005, which checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies and compiles only under `testing`. Runs in parallel with PUSH-011. File location `push_apns.rs` is an indicator.
acceptanceCriteria: Against a local HTTP/2 test server under `testing`, the request carries exactly the body and headers of the APNs row of the §10.7.1 step 5 table.
Each response row in the description maps to its outcome.
The JWT's header has `alg: ES256` and `kid`, and its claims have `iss` and `iat`.
No log line contains the key, the JWT or the device token; a test captures the tracing output.

Every end-to-end test registration goes through the signature-checking test verifier of PUSH-005, which checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies and compiles only under `testing`.
`cargo deny` passes with any new HTTP/2 dependency.

stories.title: FCM sender over the HTTP v1 API
stories.description: Reads the service-account JSON, mints an RS256 JWT for `https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token` with scope `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/firebase.messaging`, and caches the access token until 60 s before it expires (indicator). Sends the FCM row of the §10.7.1 step 5 wake-signal table to `POST https://fcm.googleapis.com/v1/projects/{project_id}/messages:send`. stories.title: Relay push startup selection and credentials
stories.description: Implements Part 5 of the plan: push selection is mandatory, has no default, and every failure is typed and fails closed (§17.17). The variable names are indicators; the rules are the contract. `SCP_RELAY_PUSH_PLATFORMS` takes `none`, `apns`, `fcm` or `apns,fcm`; `none` sets `PushRole::Disabled`. `SCP_RELAY_PUSH_STORE` has no default and is required whenever the platform list is not `none`; a shipped build accepts only `sqlite`, because the in-memory store arm compiles only under `testing` (PUSH-006). APNs needs `SCP_RELAY_APNS_KEY_PATH`, `SCP_RELAY_APNS_KEY_ID`, `SCP_RELAY_APNS_TEAM_ID`, `SCP_RELAY_APNS_TOPIC` and `SCP_RELAY_APNS_ENVIRONMENT` (`production` or `sandbox`, no default). FCM needs `SCP_RELAY_FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_PATH`, and `SCP_RELAY_FCM_PROJECT_ID` or the JSON's `project_id`. Credentials load only from file paths; key bytes, JWTs and access tokens live in zeroizing buffers; no `Debug` implementation prints them. The ADR-004 operator table records that APNs credentials bind a relay to one Apple team and topic, and FCM credentials to one Firebase project. The `scp-node` embedded relay takes the same selection through its builder, defaulting to `Disabled` and never reading credentials implicitly; the `scp-node` file path is an indicator.
acceptanceCriteria: When `SCP_RELAY_PUSH_PLATFORMS` is unset, `start_relay_from_env` returns a typed `StartupError` with an SCP-CAPSEL code.
The value `none` yields `PushRole::Disabled`.
With `apns` listed, each missing APNs variable yields its own `StartupError` variant naming that variable.
An unreadable key file, or one with group or world permissions, yields a typed error.
The same rules hold for FCM.
`SCP_RELAY_PUSH_STORE` has no default; a shipped build accepts `sqlite` and returns a typed `StartupError` for any other value, `memory` included.
When push is enabled, the relay wires `KelPushVerifier`.
A test checks that the `Debug` output of the push config struct contains no key byte, JWT or access token.
The `scp-node` builder exposes push as an explicit selection whose default is `Disabled`.

Until PUSH-033's envelope opener exists, a push-enabled relay rejects every PUBLISH at a reserved tier 3 push routing ID with `4060` and stores nothing, on every listener (§10.7.1 **Tier 3 relays**, **Tier 3 envelope**). The push gate decides this from the `bridgeTarget` of the entry whose ID the PUBLISH arrived at, so no relay configuration and no runtime change of the reservation reaches signature verification with an unopened message.
actionItems: Parse the push variables in `startup.rs` with one typed error per failure.
Load credentials from files into zeroizing buffers.
Add the ADR-004 operator table rows and the README section.
Expose the selection in the `scp-node` builder.

stories.title: Supervisor query for push routing IDs
stories.description: `Supervisor::push_routing_ids()` fans a query out to each standing context actor. Each actor returns its `context_routing_id` and this device's current `pseudonym_routing_id` (§9.10.4). The Supervisor groups the results by canonical relay URL (§9.18.2). FFI, SDK and matrix rows are covered by PUSH-015.
acceptanceCriteria: With two contexts on two relays, the result maps each relay to exactly the routing IDs of the contexts on it.
the result contains this device's current local pseudonym routing ID for each context; after the local pseudonym changes, the next query returns the new one and not the old one
The query runs `dispatch_push_command` → actor mailbox → `handlers/push.rs` → `push_helpers.rs`.
`pipeline_wiring.rs` asserts that step.

Add the `pipeline_wiring.rs` assertion.

stories.title: Runtime push registrar (build, sign, publish, deregister)
stories.description: `PushRegistrar::reconcile` reads the routing IDs from PUSH-013, compares them per relay with the set it last sent, and for each relay whose set changed builds a registration, computes its preimage through the PUSH-004 canonical-bytes function with that relay's canonical URL, signs the SHA-256 of the preimage through `KeyCustody::sign`, and publishes the message to that relay's reserved routing ID. A relay that left the set gets a `PushDeregistration` (§10.7.1 **Re-registration**). `register` and `deregister` return one result per relay, so one relay's failure does not stop the others. `refresh_token` deregisters the old token and then registers the new one (§10.7.1 **Token refresh**). A trigger task runs `reconcile` at start and whenever `Supervisor::push_routes_changed` reports a change: the supervisor bumps it when it adds or removes a context actor, and a running actor bumps it when its push routes change, which covers joins, leaves, close, expiry, tombstones and pseudonym rotation, so the rotation trigger is built here. Before its first publish to a relay, the registrar records the relay and token in a durable ledger held by an injected `ProtocolRepository` (spec 17 §17.3 `push_relay/`), and it deletes the record only when the relay accepts a deregistration or answers 4061 or 4063; `reconcile` deregisters every recorded relay that hosts no context of this device, so a lost OK or a restart leaves no registration behind. A deregistration of the current token clears the relay's last-sent set before it is published, because a relay can remove the registration and lose the OK, so `reconcile` never skips as unchanged a relay that may hold nothing. A relay that refused a request with 4xxx is not sent the same request again until its routing-ID set or the token changes. A 4062 refused only the message's `timestamp`, so the registrar sends that relay a new message after the backoff, signed with the clock's second at that time, which is above every `timestamp` it sent before; the new message is a new request under ADR-004. The task also takes a `deregister_all` command, which deregisters every recorded relay and stops registering until a `register` command. The registrar refuses `PushPlatform::WebPush` at construction with `PushError::WebPushUnsupported`, because a WebPush subscription is per relay (§10.7.1) and the registrar holds one token. The registrar maps wire codes to typed `PushError` values; 4062, 5003, 5004, every other 5xxx code and an unreachable relay are retryable, and 4060, 4061, 4063 and 4064 are not. The registrar signs only through a `PushSigningKey`, which holds a P-256 custody handle and refuses any other key type. The device's `#active` key is Ed25519 until SCP-315 lands, so this story gives `PushSigningKey` no production constructor: tests build one under `testing` from a P-256 key they register in the signature-checking test verifier of PUSH-005, and PUSH-036 adds the production constructor and the two criteria that need the device's `#active` key. Module location `push/mod.rs` is an indicator.
acceptanceCriteria: Against a relay wired with `KelPushVerifier`, `register` returns `PushError::VerifierUnavailable` for each relay.
Joining a context triggers exactly one re-registration on the affected relay, and a member event that leaves this device's routing IDs unchanged publishes nothing.
The signed bytes contain no context ID (D7); a test checks the preimage against the context ID bytes.
`pipeline_wiring.rs` has a step assertion for `push.register`, from the registrar down to the relay PUBLISH.

Preimage target field (§9.5.2 field 7 of `PushRegistration`, field 6 of `PushDeregistration`): for a relay that is not a tier 3 entry, `register` and `deregister` sign `bridge_target` = `SHA-256(0x00)`; a test checks that each signed preimage ends with those 32 bytes. A relay given as a tier 3 entry is refused with `PushError::Tier3Unsupported` and nothing is published to it; registration with a tier 3 entry is PUSH-035.

`deregister` publishes one signed `PushDeregistration` per relay, over that relay's canonical URL, and the relay removes the registration. When the device leaves its last context on a relay, `reconcile` sends that relay a `PushDeregistration` and no `PushRegistration` (§10.7.1 **Re-registration**).
`refresh_token` sends each registered relay a `PushDeregistration` for the old token and then a `PushRegistration` for the new token (§10.7.1 **Token refresh**).

Relay codes 4060, 4061, 4062, 4063, 4064, 5003 and 5004 each map to a distinct `PushError` variant. `PushError::retryable` is true for 4062, 5003, 5004, every other 5xxx code and an unreachable relay, and false for 4060, 4061, 4063 and 4064. After a 4062 the trigger task sends the relay a new message after the backoff, whose `timestamp` is above the refused one. The trigger task retries only a retryable failure, with the ADR-004 backoff of 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, 16 s and a 30 s cap, and stops on shutdown.

Each message's `timestamp` is the clock's current second, and it is above every `timestamp` the registrar sent earlier for the same relay and registration key. When the clock has not passed the last one, the registrar waits for the next second; it never sends a `timestamp` ahead of its clock (§10.7.1 **Freshness**).

The registrar signs only with a `PushSigningKey` whose custody handle holds a P-256 signing key; a handle of any other key type is refused with `PushError::SigningKeyNotP256` before anything is published. `PushSigningKey` has no constructor outside `testing` (PUSH-036 adds it).
When the routing-ID query fails, `reconcile` returns that error and publishes nothing.
`NativeRelayClient::publish_raw` returns a relay `ERR` as `TransportError::RelayRejected` carrying the relay's code, so the registrar reads the code instead of parsing text.

When a relay gets a deregistration of the current token and no OK, the next `register` command or `reconcile` that wants the relay again sends it a `PushRegistration`, also of the routing-ID set it held before.
actionItems: Write the registrar, its signing key type, and its re-registration trigger.
Map the wire codes to `PushError`.
Carry the relay's error code through `publish_raw` and write the transport push publisher.
Add the `pipeline_wiring.rs` assertion.

stories.title: FFI exports push_enable, push_disable and push_handle_wake
stories.description: Implements the call order ADR-025 criterion 4 and ADR-027 criterion 10 state. UniFFI: `push_enable(provider: PushProvider, platform)` calls `register_push()` and then the PUSH-014 registrar; `push_disable` deregisters; `push_handle_wake(payload)` calls `handle_notification`, checks the wake bytes, runs PUSH-016, and returns `WakeOutcome`. napi and Python hosts have no callback provider, so they export `push_register(platform, token)`, `push_deregister` and `push_handle_wake`, taking the token directly. Adding pipeline assertions and matrix rows only adds enforcement, which AGENTS.md allows. SDK wrappers are PUSH-017, PUSH-018 and PUSH-020. `push_enable` builds the registrar's `PushSigningKey` with the production constructor that PUSH-036 adds.

`pipeline_wiring.rs` asserts that each export reaches the registrar.
The matrix has a `Push` domain with `register`, `deregister` and `handle_wake` rows.
A UniFFI test with a Rust-side fake provider under `testing` proves that `push_enable` calls `register_push` exactly once.

Add the pipeline assertions, the conformance entries and the matrix rows.

stories.title: Device wake handling (connect and pull)
stories.description: `handle_wake(core, platform, payload)` in `scp-ffi-common` applies the §10.7.1 device receipt rule for the platform, then runs the push-wake pull mode of ADR-029 §2 under one 25-second deadline (ADR-025 criterion 4, ADR-027 criterion 10). An invalid payload returns `SCP-TRANS-5080` before any connection. The handler restores every persisted Active context that is not resident: the startup restore in a process with no known context, and each missing context alone, with no saga replay, in a process that knows one. It dials the union of the Active contexts' persisted relay URLs once, on a transient transport with cover traffic off (§9.10.6) whose connection budget is the size of that union, so it evicts no relay; it never installs that transport. It runs Phases 1, 2 and 4 for every Active context. Phase 1 queries only the relays in that context's own relay set, for the shared routing ID and each pseudonym routing ID the member holds, from the stored `sync/{context_id}/last_relay_contact` minus 5 seconds. The actor handles every pulled envelope in pull-only delivery mode, so a sender-key answer a delivered `KeyRequest` queues stays queued until the next full reconnection sends it. The pull runs no checkpoint, Update, queue drain, or Tier 2 or Tier 3 engine, so it signs, ratchets and publishes nothing, and it leaves `needs_reconnect` set. The handler writes a context's `last_relay_contact` only after Phases 2 and 4 have fed every blob of its buffer to the actor; a context that fails or that the deadline stops keeps its stored value. The outcome is `NewData` when the actor accepted at least one application envelope in any context; otherwise `Failed` when any cause ADR-029 §2 step 7 lists holds; otherwise `NoData`. A failure is a `WakeFailure` with a stable per-variant error code and a flat view for the FFI. A full reconnection reads each context's `last_relay_contact` from the store instead of taking it from the caller, reports `envelopes_delivered` and `relay_contact_error` on every bridge, sends the queued sender-key answers, and reports a Tier 3 reset only when the epoch advanced. Every native adapter connection names its cover-traffic choice. The FFI exports of `handle_wake` belong to PUSH-015.
acceptanceCriteria: With one envelope buffered on a test relay, `handle_wake` returns `NewData` and the woken member's receive buffer holds a `MessageReceived` event.
With none buffered, it returns `NoData`.
With the relay unreachable, or with a relay that accepts the WebSocket upgrade and never answers QUERY, it returns `Failed` within 26 seconds; the silent relay gives `Failed(DeadlineExpired)`.
An invalid payload for each of APNs, FCM and WebPush returns `SCP-TRANS-5080` and opens no relay connection.
A cold start over the same storage with no prior `connect` restores the contexts and returns `NewData`.
A persisted Active context whose restore fails returns `Failed`, not `NoData`, and a later wake restores a persisted Active context that is not resident even when another context is.
The woken device publishes nothing to the relay, and `needs_reconnect` stays set after the wake.
A blob addressed to the woken member's pseudonym routing ID is pulled and delivered.
The wake writes `sync/{context_id}/last_relay_contact`, and a second wake queries from the stored value minus 5 seconds.
A blob the actor refuses on the Phase 4 re-feed is not counted as delivered.
A full reconnection that clears `needs_reconnect` writes `sync/{context_id}/last_relay_contact`, and so does each envelope a live subscription delivers on every bridge that has a live delivery path.

`pipeline_wiring.rs` asserts `handle_wake` → `wake_pull_contexts` → the catch-up path, that `wake_pull_contexts` calls no checkpoint or Update builder, that the wake passes the pull-only delivery mode, and `Supervisor::wake_targets` → `PushCommand::WakeTarget` → `handlers/push.rs` → `push_helpers::wake_target`.
A peer's `KeyRequest` that a wake delivers, with the instance transport installed, makes the wake publish nothing and leaves the answer queued; the next full reconnection sends it.
When the deadline stops a wake during delivery, the context's `last_relay_contact` is unchanged and the next wake delivers the blobs the first did not.

With two contexts on disjoint relays, each relay sees queries only for its own context's routing IDs, and a dead relay that serves only one context fails that context while the other still gives `NewData`.
A wake over more relays than the Mobile connection budget (10) queries every relay and evicts none.
A full reconnection takes no caller-supplied contact map on any bridge or SDK, and every bridge reconnect result carries `envelopes_delivered`, `relay_contact_error` and `failure_code`.
A Tier 3 reconnection that receives no Welcome reports `failed`, leaves `needs_reconnect` set and writes no contact.

Creating, joining by Welcome, and importing a context each write `last_relay_contact` before the operation returns, and a failed write fails the operation without starting the actor; restoring writes nothing.
Create and import persist the context's snapshot before they start its actor, and a failed write fails the operation without starting the actor.

Create, Welcome join and import write `last_relay_contact` before the snapshot; when the operation fails or times out after a write, the snapshot and contact stored before it began are back in place, or absent where none was, and a contact is never removed while its snapshot remains. A create over the id of a running context fails and leaves that context's snapshot and contact unchanged.

A full reconnection reports a context with no stored `last_relay_contact`, or whose stored value cannot be read, as `Failed` with its own typed code, classifies no tier for it, keeps its `needs_reconnect` set, and reconnects every other context.
`WakeFailure` and each per-context pull failure carry a stable `SCP-` error code, and every failure has a unit test.
actionItems: Amend ADR-029, ADR-025 criterion 4 and ADR-027 criterion 10 with the push-wake pull mode.
Write `handle_wake` and `wake_pull_contexts` over signer-free Phase 1, 2 and 4 functions that deliver in pull-only mode.
Carry a required `DeliveryMode` on `DeliverIncoming`, and send queued sender-key answers on every full reconnection.

Add a per-relay query to `TransportManager` for the wake, keep `query` on the first adapter for every other caller, size the wake's transport to its dial set, and make the native adapter's cover-traffic choice a required parameter.

Add the `last_relay_contact` store on the runtime repository, derive it in `DurableProviders::from_handle` from the supervisor's storage handle, write it at create, Welcome join and import, advance it from the three paths, and read it in the full reconnection through the supervisor.
Add the real-relay integration tests and the wiring assertions.

stories.title: Specify the WebPush wake signal, token encoding and VAPID key publication
stories.description:
Alec ruled on 2026-10-12 (D3) that WebPush is specified fully, in its own gate after APNs and FCM. §10.7.1 lists `WebPush` in the platform enum and §22.11.4 gives it tag `0x03`, but no artifact defines its token, its request, or its receipt rule. A push service delivers a WebPush message only under RFC 8291 message encryption and RFC 8292 VAPID, so the token must carry the subscription's endpoint URL, its `p256dh` public key and its `auth` secret, and the relay must hold a VAPID key pair whose public key the browser passes to `PushManager.subscribe` as `applicationServerKey`.

This story writes the spec text. (1) §22.11.4 gives the WebPush token one canonical encoding: the endpoint as a length-prefixed UTF-8 `https` URL under §9.5.1, then `p256dh` as the 65-byte uncompressed P-256 point, then `auth` as 16 bytes; the endpoint length cap is an indicator (2048 bytes). (2) The §10.7.1 step 5 table gains a WebPush row: `POST <endpoint>` with headers `Content-Encoding: aes128gcm`, `Urgency: high`, `TTL` (indicator: 3600) and `Authorization: vapid t=<JWT>, k=<VAPID public key, base64url>`; the body is the RFC 8291 encryption of the plaintext `{"scp":"1"}` as one aes128gcm record with a fresh ephemeral key and salt per message. The VAPID JWT is ES256 with `aud` set to the endpoint's origin, `exp` at most 24 hours ahead, and `sub` set to the operator contact. (3) The device receipt rule: the decrypted data parses as a JSON object with exactly the key `scp`, whose value is the string `"1"`. (4) Browsers require `userVisibleOnly: true`, so the service worker shows a notification for every push; §10.7.1 fixes that notification's text as a constant that carries no sender, context, count or preview, which keeps §10.7's opacity. (5) A browser `PushSubscription` is bound to one `applicationServerKey`, and each relay has its own VAPID key, so §10.7.1 states how a browser with contexts on several relays holds one subscription per relay (indicator: one service-worker registration per relay, each with its own scope). (6) ADR-004 states where a relay publishes its VAPID public key (indicator: a field of the relay's handshake response) and that a relay without a VAPID key rejects a WebPush registration with 4061. (7) The endpoint is chosen by the registrant, so ADR-004 requires the relay to refuse any endpoint whose scheme is not `https` or whose host resolves to an address that is not global unicast (loopback, private, link-local, unique-local, or the relay's own addresses), with code 4060 at registration and no request sent.
acceptanceCriteria: §22.11.4 states the WebPush token encoding: length-prefixed `https` endpoint, 65-byte uncompressed `p256dh`, 16-byte `auth`, and the endpoint length cap.
The §10.7.1 step 5 table has a WebPush row giving the request line, the four headers, the VAPID JWT claims, and the encrypted body's plaintext `{"scp":"1"}` under RFC 8291 aes128gcm.

§10.7.1 step 5 states the WebPush receipt rule (a JSON object with exactly the key `scp`, whose value is the string `"1"`) and the constant notification text that carries no sender, context, count or preview.
§10.7.1 states how a browser with contexts on more than one relay holds one subscription per relay.
ADR-004 states where a relay publishes its VAPID public key, the 4061 rejection when it has none, and the endpoint refusal rule with code 4060.
The sentence "This table defines no WebPush request." is gone from §10.7.1.
`python3.12 scripts/check-doc-citations.py` passes.
actionItems: Add the WebPush token encoding to §22.11.4.
Add the WebPush row, receipt rule, notification text and per-relay subscription rule to §10.7.1.
Add the VAPID key publication and the endpoint refusal rule to ADR-004.

stories.title: WebPush sender (RFC 8291 encryption and RFC 8292 VAPID)
stories.description: Adds the `WebPush` arm of the PUSH-008 `PushSender` enum, sending the WebPush row of the §10.7.1 step 5 table (PUSH-021). Encryption follows RFC 8291: an ephemeral P-256 key pair per message, ECDH with the token's `p256dh`, the HKDF steps keyed by the token's `auth` secret, and the RFC 8188 aes128gcm content coding with a fresh 16-byte salt and one record. The VAPID JWT is ES256, signed with the relay's VAPID key through the `p256` crate the workspace already uses, and cached per endpoint origin until shortly before `exp` (indicator: 5 minutes). Before each send, the sender applies the PUSH-021 endpoint rule to the resolved address and connects to that address, so a DNS answer cannot change between the check and the request. Response mapping: 201 to `Delivered`; 404 or 410 to `InvalidToken`; 403 to `InvalidToken`, because it means the subscription was made with another `applicationServerKey`; 400, 401 or 413 to `ConfigError`; 429 or 5xx to `Transient`. Ephemeral secrets live in zeroizing buffers. End-to-end tests register through the signature-checking test verifier of PUSH-005, which checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies and compiles only under `testing`. File location `push_webpush.rs` is an indicator. **Registration checks.** At a WebPush `PushRegistration` the relay first runs the checks that need no I/O, the §22.11.4 token decode and the endpoint parse, and rejects a failure with 4060. Only after the signature verifies does it resolve the endpoint's name and apply the ADR-004 endpoint refusal rule, rejecting a refused or unresolvable endpoint with 4060 and storing nothing, so an unsigned message never makes the relay send a DNS query. A `PushDeregistration` skips the DNS check, so a device can always remove a registration. **More response rows.** A refused address and a 3xx count as `InvalidToken` (§10.7.1 **WebPush endpoint**). Any other 2xx is `Delivered`. Any other status, and a transport error, is `Transient`, so a hostile endpoint cannot produce a warning that reads as a credentials problem. A token that fails the §22.11.4 decode at send time is `InvalidToken`, and the sender sends no request for it. **Lane rule.** Registrants choose WebPush endpoints, so the WebPush drain sends concurrently up to a bound (indicator: 32 in flight) and backs off per endpoint origin after a `Transient`. One hung or failing origin therefore delays no wake to another origin. APNs and FCM keep the PUSH-008 serial drain and platform-wide back-off. **JWT cache bound.** The VAPID JWT cache holds at most a fixed number of origins (indicator: 1,024) and evicts the least recently used one.
acceptanceCriteria: The encryption reproduces the RFC 8291 Appendix A example: given its keys, salt and plaintext, the output equals the RFC's ciphertext byte for byte.

Against a local test server under `testing`, the request carries the four headers of the WebPush row, and the body decrypts with the test subscription's private key and `auth` secret to exactly `{"scp":"1"}`.
Two sends to one token use different ephemeral keys and salts.
The VAPID JWT's header has `alg: ES256`, and its claims have `aud` equal to the endpoint origin, `exp` at most 24 hours ahead, and `sub`.
An endpoint whose host resolves to a loopback, private, link-local or unique-local address gets no request, and a test proves it for each class.
Each response row in the description maps to its outcome.
No log line contains the endpoint, `p256dh`, `auth`, the VAPID key or the JWT; a test captures the tracing output.

Every end-to-end test registration goes through the signature-checking test verifier of PUSH-005, which checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies and compiles only under `testing`.
`cargo deny` passes with any new dependency.

The relay rejects with 4060, and sends no DNS query for, a WebPush registration whose token fails the §22.11.4 decode or whose endpoint is not its own WHATWG serialization; it rejects with 4060 after the signature verifies, and stores nothing for, a registration whose endpoint resolves to a refused address; a deregistration sends no DNS query.
A 3xx answer maps to `InvalidToken`, and an endpoint whose address the ADR-004 rule refuses maps to `InvalidToken` and gets no request.
A WebPush push service that never answers delays no wake to another endpoint origin, and a `Transient` from one origin delays no send to another origin.
The VAPID JWT cache serves one JWT per origin, re-mints it inside the re-mint window before `exp`, and never holds more origins than its bound.

stories.title: Browser client WebPush subscription, registration and wake
stories.description: Gives the ADR-057 in-browser client WebPush. For each relay that holds one of its contexts, the client reads the relay's VAPID public key, subscribes with `userVisibleOnly: true` and that key under the per-relay rule of PUSH-021, encodes the subscription as the PUSH-021 token, and publishes a signed registration through the PUSH-004 canonical-bytes function, signing with the browser's own identity key (ADR-057, keys on-device). It deregisters on `pushsubscriptionchange` and re-registers with the new subscription. The service worker applies the PUSH-021 receipt rule, shows the constant notification for every accepted push, and posts the wake to each open page of the app. ADR-057 gives the browser cold presence: it participates only while a page is open. So an open page runs relay catch-up on the wake, and with no page open, catch-up runs when the user opens one. A rejected payload shows the constant notification, because the browser requires one, and causes no relay connection. Module paths are indicators.

The published registration's token decodes to the subscription's endpoint, `p256dh` and `auth`, and its signature verifies under the signature-checking test verifier of PUSH-005, which checks a real P-256 signature against a key the test supplies and compiles only under `testing`.

The service worker accepts exactly `{"scp":"1"}`, and rejects a payload with an extra key, a missing `scp`, or a non-string value.
Every push, accepted or rejected, shows the same constant notification text, and a test checks that the text contains no data from the payload.
An accepted push with an open page makes that page run catch-up, and a test with one envelope buffered on a test relay sees it delivered.
The matrix `Push` rows record the TypeScript browser cells.

stories.title: Pseudonym rotation in the runtime: policy, actor trigger, persisted epoch, announcement and ordered receipt
stories.description: Implements the runtime half of pseudonym rotation, which §9.10.4.1 of the security-model spec (pseudonym rotation, the BLACK-001 mitigation) specifies; issue #366, the closed pseudonym-rotation feature issue, tracked it. PUSH-027, the rotation spec amendment, wrote every clause this story cites. A context opts into rotation through `ContextParams.pseudonym_rotation`, which context governance sets through `ModifyPseudonymRotationPolicy` (ADR-031, multi-admin governance models). Contexts that do not opt in keep the v1 static pseudonym of §9.10.4, as a per-context configuration choice and not a compatibility shim. The context actor owns rotation timing: an actor-owned timer arm, armed from persisted state like the TTL arm (ADR-049, the actor-per-context concurrency model, Decision 1 and A3), plus the membership-change trigger. The actor holds no signer and no KeyCustody, so the actor only signals that a rotation is due. PUSH-028, the rotation bridge story, builds the bridge-side driver that derives the new routing ID through `KeyCustody::derive_rotatable_pseudonym` and dispatches it back as `RotatePseudonym`. This story builds everything the driver dispatches into: the command, the fail-closed persist of the rotation state, the v2 announcement, the epoch-ordered receipt in `scp-runtime` and `scp-client`, the local-routing-ID query, and the `LocalPseudonymRotated` event. Bindings from keri: rotation reads no key state; any change to the key or secret that `pseudonym_secret` derives from (§9.10.4.A) (keri slice S12) changes every pseudonym, so no persisted routing ID is assumed to survive that change; native and browser pseudonyms differ by design (§9.10.4.A). Merge order: the PR that adds the rotation state to `ContextSnapshot` merges after PUSH-025 and rebases on it. PUSH-025 is a story not yet on main that changes `PerContextState` and `ContextSnapshot` through the same `build_snapshot_from_state`, `strip_snapshot_for_public` and governance-migration paths, and its field has no serde default. PUSH-025 stays out of `blockedBy` because `scripts/validate-prd.py` rejects a reference to a story that push.json does not contain. The push registrar's re-registration on rotation is PUSH-029, not this story. The DID-level membership-change classifier, and the rotation-due signal and record deletion on a processed membership Commit, are PUSH-030, the non-committing member story. Types and file locations named here (`RotatePseudonym`, `LocalRoutingIds`, `LocalPseudonymRotated`, `PseudonymRotationState`) are indicators. The rejoin half of the receipt-ordering criterion depends on SCP-330 in main.json, under which a non-committer learns a re-added member's role only from the governance leaves the committer carries in the Commit (§7.3.1.1 of the trust spec, ADR-066). SCP-330 is not in blockedBy, because this story can start without it and only that criterion cannot pass before it lands.
acceptanceCriteria: Opt-in (§9.10.4.1 'Rotation is opt-in'): in a context created without a rotation policy, the local routing ID equals the v1 derivation (§9.10.4), and a test clock advanced past 1000 policy periods produces zero rotation signals and an unchanged routing ID.

Policy in governance (§9.10.4.1 'Rotation policy, and where it lives'): a context created with a rotation policy persists it in `ContextParams`. An executed `ModifyPseudonymRotationPolicy` that sets or changes the policy takes effect on the next actor turn and survives restore. A non-member's or unapproved proposal leaves the policy unchanged. Context creation and the action each reject a policy that sets no trigger, and a policy whose `interval_secs` is below 600 s. An executed action that sets `None` produces zero later rotation signals, and the local routing ID stays the routing ID held before the action.

Trigger in the context actor (§9.10.4.1 'Epoch schedule'): with an interval policy and a test clock, the context actor signals 'rotation due' at `T0 + j × interval_secs` for j = 1, 2, 3, where `T0` is the context's convergent creation timestamp, with no bridge or caller action. A test clock that jumps past three boundaries while the actor is stopped yields exactly one signal after restore. With `on_membership_change`, each committed AddMember or RemoveMember yields exactly one signal on every member except the added or removed member. Because the signal channel is lossy, the actor repeats the signal until the epoch advances.

Persisted epoch (§9.10.4.1 'Rotation order and crash recovery'): after `RotatePseudonym` with epoch N+1 commits, the persisted `ContextSnapshot` holds epoch N+1, the new local routing ID, the previous routing ID with its `grace_until`, and `announce_pending`. A `RotatePseudonym` whose epoch is not the persisted epoch plus one, or not the schedule index k of the 'First v2 derivation' clause for a member with no v2 epoch yet, is rejected and changes nothing. A snapshot written before this change decodes as 'no rotation state'. If the fail-closed persist fails, the epoch, local routing ID and previous routing ID stay unchanged and no announcement is sent.

Announcement (§9.10.4.1 'Announcement wire format (v2)' and 'Announcement channel'; §25.19 Vector 58): each committed rotation sends exactly one MLS application message, published only to the shared `context_routing_id`. Its plaintext is byte-equal to the Vector 58 encoding of `pseudonym_epoch = N+1` and the new routing ID, and `announce_pending` is clear after the publish succeeds.

Vector 58 (§25.19): a test in `scp-protocol` and a native plus `wasm32` test in `scp-client-wasm` reproduce both Vector 58 byte strings, and every decision and `reason` string in the Vector 58 classifier table.

Peers record the announced routing ID (§9.10.4 announcement validation; §9.10.4.A 'no member ever recomputes a peer's pseudonym'): a native peer (`scp-runtime`) and a browser peer (`scp-client`) that receive the announcement set the sender's registry record to the announced epoch and a routing ID byte-equal to the announced `routing_id`. The test uses a custody whose routing ID no peer can compute. Their next application send addresses only the new routing ID, and each emits one `ContextEvent::PseudonymAnnounced`.

Receipt ordering (§9.10.4.1 'Receipt ordering'): an announcement with the zero sentinel, the shared `context_routing_id`, the broadcast RID, a routing ID registered to another DID, or the receiver's own current or in-grace previous routing ID is rejected and leaves the registry unchanged. A v2 announcement with a lower epoch, or with an equal epoch and a different routing ID, is rejected and leaves the registry unchanged. An equal epoch with an equal routing ID changes nothing and emits no event. A v1 announcement from a DID whose record holds a v2 epoch is rejected. Committing a member's removal or departure deletes that member's record, and the member's v2 announcement at a lower epoch after rejoining is accepted, once the receiver holds the member again by verifying and applying the governance leaves of the Commit that re-adds it (SCP-330 in main.json). The registry epochs survive snapshot and restore.

Grace end and leave (§9.10.4.1 'Transition protocol and grace' and 'Leave, close and expiry during a grace'): when the grace arm fires, the persisted previous routing ID is cleared and the actor emits a grace-end event. Leaving, closing or expiring a context during a grace discards the grace state and disarms the rotation and grace arms.

Routing-ID query and event (needed by PUSH-029): after a rotation, `Supervisor::push_routing_ids()` (PUSH-013) holds the new pseudonym routing ID and not the old one, and `LocalRoutingIds` returns the current routing ID and the in-grace previous routing ID. The supervisor event channel carries `LocalPseudonymRotated` once per committed rotation, and that event carries no routing ID.

Runtime wiring (AGENTS.md integration checklist): rotation commits through `dispatch_command` → actor mailbox → `handlers/messaging.rs` → `messaging_helpers.rs`; the local-routing-ID query runs `dispatch_query` → `handlers/queries.rs` → `queries_helpers.rs`. `pipeline_wiring.rs` asserts both steps, and asserts that the rotation helper calls `send_pseudonym_announcement`.

ADR-031, multi-admin governance models, gains `ModifyPseudonymRotationPolicy`. Docs only.

stories.title: Pseudonym rotation in the bridges: rotation driver, napi dual subscription, catch-up, SDK and matrix rows
stories.description: Implements the bridge half of pseudonym rotation (§9.10.4.1 of the security-model spec), on top of the runtime half in PUSH-026. The context actor holds no KeyCustody, so a bridge-side driver in `scp-ffi-common`, modelled on `heartbeat_scheduler.rs`, holds a weak Supervisor reference, the custody, the identity key handle and a cancel token. On a 'rotation due' signal or on start, the driver reads `LocalRoutingIds`, calls `derive_rotatable_pseudonym` at the next epoch, and dispatches `RotatePseudonym`. At start it also runs the §9.10.4.1 re-derivation check for a change of the pseudonym-secret source and re-publishes a pending announcement. napi `context_subscribe_on` replaces its one-time pseudonym subscription with the routing-ID set that `LocalRoutingIds` returns, re-read on rotation and grace-end events and on a periodic tick, and spawns and tears down the driver next to the heartbeat scheduler. Reconnect catch-up covers the same set, which also changes what PUSH-016, device wake handling, pulls. UniFFI (whose `context_subscribe` is a stub) and PyO3 (which has no subscribe loop) export only the policy through `ContextParams` and the governance action, and the capability matrix records their dual-subscription rows as exemptions. Per the plan's PR split, the dual-subscription, restore-subscription and napi/matrix wiring criteria move here from PUSH-026. The custody-call, pseudonym-secret-source and destroyed-identity criteria also move here, because the driver this story builds is the only caller of the custody. Type and file names (`pseudonym_rotation_scheduler.rs`) are indicators.
acceptanceCriteria: Custody call only (§9.10.4.1 'Custody compatibility'; keri ruling): a counting custody double records exactly one `derive_rotatable_pseudonym` call per rotation, with `pseudonym_epoch` = persisted epoch + 1, and no other custody or key-state read. For identity seed 0x01×32 at epoch 1 the new routing ID equals the §25.19 Vector 30 v2 routing ID.

First v2 derivation (§9.10.4.1 'First v2 derivation, at join and when rotation is enabled'): a member that joins a context whose interval policy puts the test clock at schedule index k = 3 derives its routing ID with v2 at epoch 3. A v1 member of a live context on which governance enables rotation keeps its v1 routing ID until its next trigger, and that rotation derives v2 at the schedule index k of that moment.

Dual subscription, then drop (§9.10.4.1 'Transition protocol and grace'): from rotation until rotation time + 600 s, the napi subscribe loop holds subscriptions on both the old and the new routing ID, and a blob published to the old routing ID during the grace is delivered. Once the grace elapses, `TransportManager::unsubscribe` is called with the old routing ID, and a blob published to it afterwards is not delivered.

Restore and crash (§9.10.4.1 'Rotation order and crash recovery'): at each kill point the clause enumerates (after persist and before subscribe; after subscribe and before announce), a restore leaves the member subscribed to the new routing ID, and to the old one until its persisted `grace_until`, and the member re-publishes the announcement exactly once when `announce_pending` is set. A restore after `grace_until` subscribes only to the new routing ID.

Change of the pseudonym-secret source (§9.10.4.1 'Change of the pseudonym-secret source'; keri ruling S12): on restore, and on any change to the key or secret that `pseudonym_secret` derives from (§9.10.4.A), a member whose derivation at the persisted epoch differs from the persisted local routing ID rotates to epoch N+1, keeps the persisted routing ID subscribed for the grace, and announces. In a v1 context the member subscribes to and re-announces its new v1 routing ID. No code path treats the persisted routing ID as current without re-deriving it.

Destroyed identity (§9.10.4.A 'Destruction'): after the identity is destroyed, the driver's derive fails with key-not-found (SCP-CRYPTO-4006). The context keeps its epoch and routing ID, sends no announcement, and stays subscribed.

Leave, close and expiry (§9.10.4.1 'Leave, close and expiry during a grace'): leaving, closing or expiring a context during a grace calls `TransportManager::unsubscribe` for both the current and the previous routing ID, and stops the driver.

Reconnect catch-up (§9.10.4.1 'Reconnect catch-up'): a reconnect during a grace queries the shared `context_routing_id`, the current routing ID and the previous routing ID, and a blob stored on the previous routing ID while the member was offline is delivered.

Bridge wiring (AGENTS.md integration checklist): `pipeline_wiring.rs` asserts that the driver calls `derive_rotatable_pseudonym` and `rotate_pseudonym`, and that napi `context_subscribe_on` spawns and tears down the driver and calls `unsubscribe`. The capability matrix lists the rotation policy for every binding and records napi-only dual subscription, with exemptions for UniFFI (stub `context_subscribe`) and PyO3 (no subscribe loop). The TypeScript, Python, Kotlin and Swift SDKs expose the policy field and the policy `EventType` string.

Replace the napi one-time pseudonym subscription with the `LocalRoutingIds` set, and spawn and tear down the driver from `context_subscribe_on`.

Export the policy through the UniFFI and PyO3 `ContextParams` and the governance action.
Add the SDK policy fields and `EventType` strings, the `pipeline_wiring.rs` assertions and the capability-matrix rows.

stories.title: Push registrar re-registers on pseudonym rotation
stories.description: Verifies and pins the pseudonym-rotation path of the PUSH-014 push registrar, so that a relay wakes a device for its current pseudonym routing ID after a rotation (§10.7.1 **Re-registration**; §9.10.4.1 pseudonym rotation). PUSH-014 built the trigger: a context actor compares its push routes (`push_helpers::push_routes`) at the top of every run-loop turn and, when they changed, bumps the Supervisor's `push_routes_changed` watch, and the registrar task reconciles on every bump. A committed local rotation changes the actor's local pseudonym routing ID, so it reaches the registrar through that watch; PUSH-014 tests one rotation on one relay. This story adds what remains on top of the watch. A rotation of a context hosted on several relays re-registers on each of them once. The end of a rotation's grace changes no push route, because `push_routes` lists the current pseudonym only (the grace routing ID belongs to the wake target, not to the registration), so it publishes nothing. A watch coalesces bumps instead of dropping them, and the registrar marks the watch seen before it reads the routes, so a second rotation committed while a reconcile runs causes one more reconcile, and the relay ends holding the newest routing ID. `pipeline_wiring.rs` pins the path from the actor's route check to the registrar's reconcile. Module locations are indicators.
acceptanceCriteria: A committed rotation of a context hosted on two relays sends each of those relays exactly one `PushRegistration`, holding the new pseudonym routing ID and not the old one, and sends a third relay, which hosts only another context of the device, nothing.
The end of a rotation's grace period, after the registrar has registered the new routing ID, publishes nothing.

Two rotations committed in quick succession, the second while the registrar's reconcile for the first is still publishing, leave the relay's last accepted `PushRegistration` holding the second rotation's routing ID, with no registration of the first one after it.

`pipeline_wiring.rs` asserts the step from the actor run loop to `push.register`: `ContextActor::run` calls `note_push_route_change`, which calls `SupervisorHandle::note_push_routes_changed`, which calls `Supervisor::note_push_routes_changed`; and the registrar task's `routes.changed()` arm leads to `reconcile`.

stories.title: Non-committing members rotate on a processed membership Commit
stories.description: Implements the membership trigger of §9.10.4.1 of the security-model spec (pseudonym rotation, the BLACK-001 mitigation) for a member that did not commit the membership change. §9.10.4.1 'Epoch schedule' states that the member that commits an AddMember or RemoveMember rotates after it commits, and that every other member rotates when it processes the Commit that applies the change; it also states the membership-change criterion, which counts changes by DID and not by MLS leaf. A Commit is an AddMember for each DID that held no leaf before the Commit, and a RemoveMember for each DID whose last leaf the Commit removes. A Commit that adds or removes a device leaf of a DID that holds another leaf before and after the Commit is neither. A removed member does not rotate, and a Commit that applies several membership changes triggers one rotation. §9.10.4.1 'Receipt ordering', in its record-lifetime rule, also has a member that processes a RemoveMember Commit delete the removed DID's pseudonym-registry record. This story builds the DID-level classifier over the leaf sets before and after a Commit, and calls it on the path where the context actor processes an incoming Commit (`DeliverIncoming`, which merges the staged Commit), so that processing emits the rotation-due signal and deletes the record. PUSH-026, the runtime rotation story, owns the rotation-due signal's consumer, the committer's trigger, the timer arms and `RotatePseudonym`, and is blocked by this story. Types and file locations named here are indicators. The rejoin half of the record-deletion criterion depends on SCP-330 in main.json, under which a non-committer learns a re-added member's role only from the governance leaves the committer carries in the Commit (§7.3.1.1 of the trust spec, ADR-066); a role assumed at the receiver is a fail-open that criterion forbids. SCP-330 is not in blockedBy, because this story can start without it and only that criterion cannot pass before it lands.
acceptanceCriteria: Non-committer trigger (§9.10.4.1 'Epoch schedule', membership trigger and membership-change criterion): in a context whose policy sets `on_membership_change`, a member that did not commit an AddMember or a RemoveMember emits exactly one rotation-due signal when it processes the Commit that applies that change, and a Commit that adds a second device leaf for a DID that already holds a leaf yields zero signals. Test: a two-node test in which node A creates the context, node B joins by Welcome, and A adds and then removes a third identity C; B emits one rotation-due signal when it processes the Commit adding C and one when it processes the Commit removing C. The device-leaf rule is asserted on the DID classifier, because step 1.6 of §7.3.1.1 of the trust spec admits no Commit that adds a leaf for a member without removing one: an `AddMember` Add binds a non-member, and a Commit with no proposal that carries an Add re-adding no removed member is rejected. Test: leaf sets before and after a Commit in which C holds a leaf on both sides, one with a second leaf added beside C's and one with C's leaf removed and re-added, each classify as no membership change. Test: A executes a `ResetMember` for C, which is one Commit holding the Remove of C's leaf and the Add of C's fresh leaf (step 1.6 of §7.3.1.1); B processes that Commit and emits no rotation-due signal, and B's persisted rotation trigger is unchanged.

Record deletion on a processed Commit (§9.10.4.1 'Receipt ordering', record lifetime): in the same two-node test, after B processes A's Commit removing C, B's pseudonym registry holds no record for C's DID, and B accepts a v2 announcement from C at a lower epoch after C rejoins. B holds C as a member after C rejoins only by verifying and applying the governance leaves of the Commit that re-adds C, per SCP-330 in main.json and §7.3.1.1 of the trust spec; the test builds that Commit with its governance leaf block and asserts no role was assigned to C at B by any other path.

Call the classifier on the incoming-Commit processing path, emit one rotation-due signal per Commit that applies at least one membership change when the policy sets `on_membership_change` and the local member is not the removed member, and delete each removed DID's registry record.
Add the two-node integration test with the Welcome join, the add and remove of C, and the extra device leaf.
